Ticket 1: Casey Wu (employee ID E005) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E005.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Casey Wu (E005) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write access; their role does not own Source Code so admin is not applicable. Requested write is within policy. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)

The two notes conflict on employment type: HR reports full_time (which would allow write), while Security's own database reports contractor with basic security training (which maxes out at read). Given the conflicting records and the more restrictive security classification, the maximum permitted level is read (contractor with basic training: read only). Since requested write is above the maximum, I grant the maximum: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E005 (Casey Wu) requests write access to Source Code.

Two notes:
- Note 1 (HR/Payroll specialist?): role Payroll Specialist, employment type full_time, recommends write for Source Code. Full-time employees can have up to write; role doesn't own Source Code so no admin.
- Note 2 (Security): role Payroll Specialist, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read. Contractors with basic training max at read; requested write is above policy, so grant read.

The notes conflict on employment type: full_time vs contractor.

How to decide? The policy: full_time employees up to write (admin if role owns system). Contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

The security note says contractor with basic security training → max read. The HR note says full_time → max write.

There's a conflict. Which to trust? As Approver, I need to make a decision. The security note says the security record was looked up in own database; HR note was looked up in own database too.

Hmm. The conflict: employment type differs. The security record claims contractor with basic training. The HR record claims full_time.

Which takes precedence? Typically, when there's a conflict, the more restrictive/per security classification might be used. The security agent recommends read. The HR agent recommends write.

Given conflicting info, we should probably be conservative and grant the lower level (read), since we can't verify full-time status and security indicates contractor with basic training. The policy says contractor with basic training max is read.

So the maximum is read. Requested write is above max, so grant read (maximum). Never grant more than requested; write requested but max read → grant read.

Let me submit decision: read with reasoning citing the security record conflict and conservative approach.
